To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) implementation teams used an electronic information management systems (PHIMS), as well as additional informal tools and technology to support their implementation work; (ii) the informal tools enabled teams to create locally derived knowledge about how to deliver the program and how to use PHIMS; and (iii) the use of the informal tools complemented and supported the use of PHIMS.

(1) practitioners use a range of tools to manage and curate knowledge about implementation; (2) these tools complement formal systems, enabling practitioners to develop locally relevant knowledge about how to implement programs and to share that knowledge with their team; and (3) the content of the knowledge is context specific, but the function of the tools may be more broadly applicable.
implementation involves knowing and formalising what to do, and how to do it, and that this knowledge can only be generated and managed by practitioners in the local context.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding and supporting implementation knowledge and its management, and the implications of this for the design and use of information management systems.
the science of how to get programs into practice and how to manage and support the people doing this.
the role of informal knowledge in the implementation of large-scale programs and the implications for system design.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the implementation of evidence-based programs is a complex process involving the generation of locally relevant knowledge and the use of multiple tools, including formal and informal tools, to manage this knowledge and coordinate implementation activities.
the use of informal tools and technologies in implementation is a critical factor to consider when designing systems that support implementation.
the use of PHIMS and other informal tools and technologies is an important part of how implementers generate, curate, store and manage knowledge for program implementation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
implementation science requires the integration of formal and informal systems, which can be achieved through a focus on local implementation knowledge and its management.

the successful implementation of evidence-based programs is not just about the program itself but also requires the creation and management of supplementary knowledge to support the program in the field, which can be supported by a range of tools, both formal and informal.
implementation science requires the study of how implementers generate, manage and apply knowledge to do implementation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
implementation knowledge is not only about knowing what to do but also about how to do it and how to do it in a way that can be documented and formalized.
implementation knowledge needs to be understood in terms of the local context and the multiple relationships and accountabilities that are part of it.
the science of implementation needs a more nuanced understanding of the knowledge required to deliver evidence-based programs in practice.
